In class five, Ishita got stuck on the word "environment" while reading aloud. Her tongue tied itself, and a hot flush crept up her neck. She wobbled her head like a broken toy and pulled her mouth into a wide, silly shape. The class roared, and Gurpreet Ma'am bit back a smile before asking her to try again. Ishita grinned and bowed to the class, but under the desk she was twisting her hem into a knot.
At fifteen, Ishita came out of the last period and dropped her bag on the bench. "Ugh." Jomon, waiting for her, frowned. "Was that at me?" Ishita blinked, then realised how it had sounded. "No, no. Sorry. Ugh, what a draining day. Two tests and a fight with the printer." Jomon relaxed and held out half his samosa. "Should've said so." Ishita bit into it, laughing. From then on, when a day went badly, she tried to put a few words after the sound so nobody had to guess.

qa.q: Which word did Ishita stumble on while reading aloud in class five?
qa.a: She got stuck on the word "environment".

qa.q: How are the silly face at ten and the "Ugh" at fifteen alike, and how did Ishita change?
qa.a: Both are quick ways to control a moment: at ten Ishita wobbled her head and pulled her mouth into a silly shape, and at fifteen she said Ugh. When Jomon asked if it was at him, she put a few words after the sound so nobody had to guess.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she grinned and bowed but twisted her hem into a knot?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and worried underneath, and the clowning helped her stay in control of the moment.

qa.q: What could Jomon do when someone's short sound leaves him unsure?
qa.a: He can ask calmly, as he did with "Was that at me?", and then listen to the answer without taking offence.

grounding: A class clown's joke covering embarrassment (3891) and a teen's 'ugh' that is softened with a few words (2527): both are ways to manage a feeling, at different ages.

passage:
At twenty, Ira sat in the seminar room of a top institute, certain she had been admitted by luck. She watched classmates argue with ease and told her friend Mridul that any day now someone would notice the mistake. When a professor praised her essay, she shrugged. "The topic was easy." Later she compared her notes with others' and thought hers looked smaller.
At twenty-four, Ira started at a research firm. For two weeks she had nodded at a term nobody explained, afraid that asking would prove she did not belong. On Thursday, standing beside Harsha's desk, she finally said, "Sorry, what does 'baseline' mean here?" Her heart thumped. Harsha turned from the screen. "Oh, that's just the starting figure we compare against. It confuses everyone at first. Want me to send you the glossary?" That was all. No sigh, no sideways look. Ira thanked Harsha and walked back to her seat slowly, surprised at how light her shoulders felt.

qa.q: What word did Ira ask Harsha to explain?
qa.a: She asked what "baseline" meant.

qa.q: How does the reply from Harsha at twenty-four challenge the belief Ira held at twenty?
qa.a: At the institute Ira believed she was there by luck and told Mridul someone would notice the mistake. At the firm she nodded at a term for two weeks, but when Harsha answered her question kindly, with no sigh and no sideways look, her shoulders felt light and the fear that she did not belong began to loosen.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling with her heart thumping before she asked about "baseline"?
qa.a: She was nervous and afraid of being judged, expecting that a basic question would reveal she did not belong.

qa.q: What could Ira do next time she meets a term she does not know?
qa.a: She can ask right away, and keep a glossary or notes, since a plain question is usually answered kindly and matter-of-factly.

grounding: Fraud feelings at a top college (4092) begin to loosen at a new job when a basic question gets a kind, matter-of-fact reply (3232); one person over years.

At ten, Kunal stumbled over a line in the reading and the class went quiet. He crossed his eyes and announced, in a booming voice, that the book had bitten his tongue. Everyone laughed, and Himani Ma'am shook her head with a small smile. Kunal laughed loudest, though his fingers tapped the desk rapidly.
Ten years later, Simran sat two rows behind him in a college lecture, thinking of the jokes he threw into every discussion. He was funny, sure of himself, and always in the middle of a group. After three chats at the canteen she had already pictured them travelling together and going to each other's family functions. One evening she asked about his plans after graduation. Kunal grinned. "Plans? I plan to have a very nice sandwich." The group laughed, and Simran laughed with them. Somewhere in the back of her mind she wondered if the easy confidence was the whole of him. She pushed the thought away and went on imagining the trip.

qa.q: What did Kunal claim had happened when he stumbled over the reading?
qa.a: He announced that the book had bitten his tongue.

qa.q: How does Simran's view of Kunal in college connect to his behaviour at ten?
qa.a: At ten Kunal crossed his eyes and joked when he was embarrassed, while his fingers tapped the desk. In college Simran sees only the funny, confident Kunal in the middle of a group and pictures them travelling together, so the person she imagines is partly the one she wishes for.

qa.q: What might Simran be feeling as she pushes the thought about his confidence away?
qa.a: She feels excited and infatuated, but also a small doubt she would rather not look at.

qa.q: What could Simran do to get to know Kunal better before imagining more?
qa.a: She could talk with him in quieter settings, notice how he handles stress and unfunny topics, and let the picture of him grow from what she really sees.

grounding: A child's joke covering embarrassment (3891) and a later classmate drawn to that same humour and confidence, filling in the rest with wishes (2998).

On Tuesday, Anirban said to his mother, "Mummy, I'll finish my drawing in ten minutes, well before we eat." He got out all his colours and began a big picture of a train station. At the first hour he was still adding tiny windows. When Mummy Preeti called him for dinner, he wailed that it was not done yet, and his eyes filled with tears as he left the page half-coloured.
On Wednesday, Sonali Ma'am reminded the class that the science project on plants was due on Friday. "That will take me ten minutes," Anirban told his friend. He did not begin on Wednesday, and he did not begin on Thursday afternoon. On Thursday night, at eight o'clock, he opened the chart paper and found he had no glue, no pictures and no idea where to begin. He remembered how easy the plan had looked in his head, while the paper in front of him looked huge. Mummy Preeti found him at the table at nine, sighing, with the pen cap in his mouth. Nobody had told him to think of Tuesday's drawing, and he had not remembered it himself.

qa.q: What did Anirban tell his mother he would finish before dinner?
qa.a: He said he would finish his drawing in ten minutes.

qa.q: How do Tuesday's drawing and Thursday night's project show the same mistake?
qa.a: Both times Anirban imagined a task taking ten minutes and pictured the easy path. On Tuesday the drawing stretched to an hour and ended in tears; on Thursday he began the plant project late and forgot how long the drawing had really taken.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when Mummy Preeti called him to dinner with the drawing unfinished?
qa.a: He felt upset and frustrated, because he had expected to be done and now had to stop halfway.

qa.q: What could Anirban do next time he plans a task?
qa.a: He could remember how long the drawing really took, add extra time, and begin the project earlier in small parts.

grounding: The same boy imagines a task will take ten minutes (3650) and it stretches into an hour with tears (7655), then repeats the misjudgement on a school project.

The history assignment sat in Gurpreet's bag for a week. Every time it came to mind, a knot tightened: if the essay was weak, Parul Ma'am would know Gurpreet was not as sharp as everyone said. So on Monday Gurpreet said "tomorrow" and switched to a football video. The knot loosened at once, and the room felt lighter. Shalini messaged, "Did you start?" Gurpreet replied with a laughing face and went back to the video.
On Tuesday it happened again, and the lift felt just as sweet. By Wednesday night, though, a quiet hum of guilt ran under everything, even a game with cousins. Each time Gurpreet skipped the task, the relief arrived faster, which made skipping more tempting. On Thursday morning, Gurpreet rushed three paragraphs on the bus, copied a date wrong and handed the essay in feeling ill. Parul Ma'am's comment, when it came, said the ideas showed promise but the work looked hurried. Gurpreet read it twice, wishing the essay could have been the one from the first Monday.

qa.q: Which day did Gurpreet first say "tomorrow" and switch to a football video?
qa.a: Gurpreet did this on Monday.

qa.q: How do the relief and guilt help explain why Gurpreet's essay ended up weak?
qa.a: Skipping the task gave an immediate lift, followed by a hum of guilt, and the relief rewarded the avoiding, so it happened again and again. The underlying fear of judgement was never faced, and the rushed essay was worse than one written earlier.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when the football video loosened the knot?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt sudden relief from the fear of a weak essay, though the fear itself was still there.

qa.q: What could Shalini do to help without adding pressure?
qa.a: Shalini could offer to sit and work together for a short spell, and tell Gurpreet that a rough first draft is fine.

grounding: Putting off the essay to avoid judgement (4056) is rewarded by relief and followed by guilt (3189), strengthening the pattern.

passage:
At five, Akash pulled at Mummy Ganga's dupatta ten minutes after finishing his snack. "I'm bored. Can I watch cartoons?" Mummy did not switch on the screen. She gave him a tray of wet sand from the balcony pot, a spoon and a few leaves. He sighed, then began to dig a road for a leaf-boat, and by evening his bedroom floor was full of little roads.
At nine, Akash sat on the sofa after homework with nothing planned. Without thinking, his thumb found the phone and began to scroll. Videos slid by, one after another. After half an hour, he noticed he had not laughed once and felt a bit grumpy. He remembered the leaf-boat roads. He put the phone down on the cushion, took a pencil and began drawing a map of an island. When his neighbour Uday called from the ground floor, Akash grabbed the pad and ran down, and the two of them spent the evening making the island a real one out of sand and sticks.

qa.q: What did Mummy Ganga give Akash instead of switching on cartoons?
qa.a: She gave him a tray of wet sand, a spoon and a few leaves.

qa.q: How does Akash's boredom at nine differ from his boredom at five, and what stays the same?
qa.a: At five, Akash asked for cartoons but when given sand and leaves his boredom became a game. At nine, his thumb went to the phone on its own, but he noticed he felt grumpy and chose a pencil and outdoors instead, so boredom still led to new ideas.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling after half an hour of scrolling?
qa.a: He felt flat and a bit grumpy, since the videos had not made him laugh even once.

qa.q: What could Akash's family do to help him choose an activity over the phone?
qa.a: They could keep pencils, paper and outdoor things within reach and give him unstructured time after homework without scolding him.

grounding: A child's boredom that turns to imagination with simple materials (4068) and the same child at nine choosing drawing and play over scrolling (890).
